name: Vietnam
tagline: Karst bays, lantern towns, pho at dawn.
overview: Vietnam rewards travellers who like their trips layered. The country runs 1,600km top to bottom, and each stretch feels like a different holiday: limestone islands rising out of Ha Long Bay in the north, lantern-lit merchant houses and tailor shops in Hoi An at the centre, and the caffeinated, scooter-swarmed energy of Ho Chi Minh City in the south. Food is the connective tissue — a bowl of pho at a pavement stall costs less than a Delhi metro ride and outclasses most restaurant meals back home. For Indian travellers the logistics have never been easier: non-stop flights of about five hours from Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata, an e-visa sorted online in days, and a dong that stretches a mid-range budget into balcony rooms and private guides. The one mistake to avoid is trying to see it all in a week — pick north or centre-south, and save the rest for the return trip you will inevitably plan.

quickFacts.flightFromIndia: ≈5h non-stop from Delhi, Mumbai or Kolkata to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City
quickFacts.plug: Type A/C · 220V — most Indian round-pin plugs fit; carry one universal adapter to be safe
quickFacts.sim: Viettel or Mobifone tourist eSIM from about ₹500–700 for 15–30 days of generous data

visa.headline: E-visa · up to 90 days
visa.body: Indian passport holders apply online at the official evisa.gov.vn portal — no embassy visit, no biometrics. Choose single or multiple entry, upload a passport scan and photo, and pay by card. Print the approved PDF and carry it; airlines check it at boarding. Apply at least 10 days before flying to leave buffer.
visa.cost: USD 25 single entry (≈₹2,200) · USD 50 multiple entry

weather.summary: Three climate zones stacked in one country: the north has a proper cool winter and a hot, wet summer; the central coast is sunny February to August then stormy; the tropical south splits simply into dry and rainy. Somewhere in Vietnam is always in season — the trick is matching your route to the month.

seasons.label: Cool & dry
seasons.notes: Crisp, clear weather in Hanoi and Ha Long, dry beach days in the south — the whole country at its most comfortable.

seasons.label: Shoulder
seasons.notes: Warm and mostly dry countrywide, with the central beaches hitting their stride and rates a notch softer.

seasons.label: Wet season
seasons.notes: Hot and humid with afternoon downpours in the north and south; central Vietnam stays sunniest, but Sep–Nov brings typhoon risk to that coast.

booking.high: Dec – Feb, plus Tet (Lunar New Year, usually late Jan – mid Feb)
booking.note: Tet is the one date to plan around — trains, flights and half the shops shut for nearly a week while prices spike. Book November trips by September; Ha Long cruises and Hoi An boutique stays sell out first.

idealDuration.note: Seven nights does the north properly — Hanoi, Ninh Binh and a Ha Long cruise — or Da Nang, Hoi An and Hue. Nine lets you fly south and add Ho Chi Minh City or Phu Quoc.

budget.note: Per person per day with mid-range hotels, Grab rides and one paid activity. Vietnam undercuts Thailand and Bali on almost everything — four-star rooms in Hoi An start around ₹3,500 a night.

safety.headline: Very safe for tourists — petty theft and traffic are the real risks
tips: Hold phones and bags on the kerb side of the pavement; drive-by snatching happens in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.
Cross roads at a slow, steady walk — scooters flow around you, but never step back or sprint.
Use Grab for taxis and bike rides; it kills meter disputes and shows the fare upfront.
Agree prices before hopping into cyclos or buying from street vendors in tourist zones.
Ride a scooter only with an IDC-endorsed licence and helmet — insurance will not cover you otherwise.
Stick to bottled or filtered water, and pick busy street-food stalls where turnover keeps things fresh.

goodToKnow: Cash still rules at markets and street stalls — carry small dong notes; ₫500,000 and ₫20,000 notes look confusingly similar, so check twice.
Tipping is not expected, though rounding up or ₫50,000 for a guide is appreciated.
Grab works for cars, bikes and food delivery in every major city; download it before landing.
Vegetarians should learn 'an chay' (vegetarian) — Buddhist com chay eateries exist in every town and Indian restaurants are common in big cities.
The overnight sleeper trains and open-tour buses between cities are comfortable and cheap; domestic VietJet flights often cost under ₹3,000 if booked early.
Tet (Lunar New Year) transforms the country for a week — magical atmosphere, but transport and restaurants largely shut down.
Coffee is a national event: try ca phe sua da (iced with condensed milk) and Hanoi's egg coffee at least once.
Temples and Ho Chi Minh's mausoleum require covered shoulders and knees; queues at the mausoleum move fast but photography inside is banned.

cities.name: Hanoi
cities.blurb: The thousand-year-old capital where French villas, ancient pagodas and motorbike chaos share the same lakeside blocks. Base here for the Old Quarter, egg coffee and day trips to Ninh Binh and Ha Long.

image.alt: Motorbikes and shophouses on a busy Hanoi Old Quarter street

cities.name: Hoi An
cities.blurb: A perfectly preserved trading port of yellow merchant houses, silk lanterns and riverside cafés, with An Bang beach ten minutes away. The prettiest town in Vietnam and the best place to slow down.

image.alt: Silk lanterns glowing over the Thu Bon river in Hoi An's ancient town

cities.name: Ho Chi Minh City
cities.blurb: Vietnam's commercial engine — rooftop bars, war museums, Ben Thanh market and ten million scooters. The gateway to the Cu Chi Tunnels and Mekong Delta, and the country's best-value nightlife.

image.query: ho chi minh city skyline night
image.alt: Ho Chi Minh City skyline with Bitexco tower lit up at night

cities.name: Da Nang
cities.blurb: A modern beach city between Hoi An and Hue, with a long sandy coastline, the Marble Mountains and the Ba Na Hills cable car. Handy airport hub with resort strips at Indian-friendly prices.

image.alt: Da Nang's Dragon Bridge with the city and My Khe beach beyond

cities.name: Ninh Binh
cities.blurb: Ha Long Bay's scenery moved inland — limestone towers over rice paddies, rowing-boat rides through river caves at Trang An, and viewpoints like Hang Mua. Doable as a Hanoi day trip, better overnight.

image.alt: View over karst peaks and the Ngo Dong river from Hang Mua, Ninh Binh

cities.name: Phu Quoc
cities.blurb: Vietnam's island escape off the southern coast — white-sand beaches, over-water cable car to Hon Thom, and resorts that cost half their Thai equivalents. Add it as a beach finale to a southern route.

image.alt: Sunset over a white-sand beach with fishing boats on Phu Quoc island

highlights.name: Ha Long Bay overnight cruise
highlights.blurb: Nearly two thousand limestone islands rising from jade water — Vietnam's signature image, best seen from the deck of an overnight boat.
highlights.detail: Skip the rushed day trip from Hanoi and book a one-night cruise; the bay is at its best at sunset and sunrise, after the day boats leave. Mid-range boats from about ₹8,000 per person include meals, kayaking and a cave visit; luxury lines like Heritage or Indochine roughly double that. Consider Lan Ha Bay, the quieter southern section with the same karsts and fewer boats. Transfers from Hanoi take 2.5 hours on the expressway. Book December–February sailings well ahead, and keep a buffer day — cruises occasionally cancel for storms in late summer.

image.alt: A wooden cruise boat among limestone karst islands in Ha Long Bay

highlights.name: Hoi An Ancient Town
highlights.blurb: A UNESCO-listed trading port frozen in the 18th century, where lantern-lit evenings by the river are the whole point of the visit.
highlights.detail: Buy the ₫120,000 heritage ticket, which covers five of the old houses, assembly halls and the Japanese Covered Bridge. Explore at 7am when the streets belong to locals and photographers, retreat to the beach or a café through the midday heat, then return after dark when thousands of lanterns come on. On the 14th of each lunar month the town switches off electric lights entirely. Get clothes tailored on day one so fittings finish before you leave — 24-hour turnarounds are routine. Three nights here is the sweet spot, with Ba Na Hills and My Son as day trips.

image.alt: The Japanese Covered Bridge and lantern-lit streets of Hoi An at dusk

highlights.name: Hanoi Old Quarter & Train Street
highlights.blurb: Thirty-six ancient guild streets of street food, silk and scooters, with a working railway squeezing between café tables twice a day.
highlights.detail: Walk it early: Hoan Kiem Lake fills with tai chi groups before 7am, and the wet markets on Gia Ngu street are at full tilt. Graze as you go — bun cha (Obama's famous lunch spot is on Le Van Huu), banh mi 25, and egg coffee at Cafe Giang. Train Street cafés reopen intermittently under city rules; check timings locally and follow staff instructions when the train passes within arm's reach. Cap the evening with a water-puppet show near the lake and beer hoi on Ta Hien corner, where a fresh draught costs about ₹35.

image.alt: A train passing within touching distance of cafés on Hanoi's Train Street

highlights.name: Trang An & Hang Mua, Ninh Binh
highlights.blurb: Rowing boats glide through river caves beneath limestone towers, then 500 steps at Hang Mua earn the best viewpoint in northern Vietnam.
highlights.detail: Take the Trang An boat ride over the more touristy Tam Coc — rowers loop through grottoes and past cliff-top temples for about ₹1,100, choosing from three routes; route 3 balances caves and temples best. Go at 7.30am to beat both the heat and the crowds. Climb Hang Mua's dragon-spine viewpoint in late afternoon for softer light over the paddies, greenest in May–June and golden just before the harvest. Stay overnight in a Tam Coc homestay among the rice fields rather than day-tripping from Hanoi; the valley at dawn, before the buses arrive, is the reason to come.

image.query: trang an boat cave ninh binh
image.alt: Rowing boats entering a river cave beneath limestone cliffs at Trang An

highlights.name: Golden Bridge, Ba Na Hills
highlights.blurb: The bridge held aloft by two giant stone hands, floating above the clouds at 1,400m — reached by one of the world's longest cable cars.
highlights.detail: The bridge sits inside the Sun World Ba Na Hills park above Da Nang; the roughly ₹3,200 ticket bundles the spectacular 20-minute cable car, the French village, gardens and the indoor Fantasy Park. Arrive for the first cars at 8am — by 10am tour groups own the bridge, and clouds often roll in after lunch and erase the view. It runs noticeably cooler up top, so carry a layer. Budget half a day and pair it with the Marble Mountains on the way back to Hoi An or Da Nang. Skip it in heavy rain; the whole point is the panorama.

image.query: golden bridge ba na hills hands
image.alt: The Golden Bridge held up by giant stone hands above the clouds at Ba Na Hills

highlights.name: Cu Chi Tunnels & War Remnants Museum
highlights.blurb: Crawl through the guerrilla tunnel network outside Ho Chi Minh City, then let the war museum recalibrate everything you thought you knew.
highlights.detail: Do them as one themed day from Ho Chi Minh City. Cu Chi is 90 minutes away — choose the Ben Duoc site over Ben Dinh for smaller crowds and a more authentic section of the 250km network. Widened tunnel segments let visitors crawl 20–100 metres; skip them if you are claustrophobic, the ground-level exhibits still land. Half-day tours with a guide run about ₹1,500–2,500, and the speedboat option up the Saigon River is a fun upgrade. Visit the War Remnants Museum in the city afterwards — allow two quiet hours; the photography galleries are heavy but essential context.

image.alt: A guide demonstrating a hidden trapdoor entrance at the Cu Chi Tunnels

highlights.name: Mekong Delta
highlights.blurb: A watery world of floating markets, coconut orchards and sampan rides through palm-shaded canals, two hours south of Ho Chi Minh City.
highlights.detail: Day trips to My Tho and Ben Tre from Ho Chi Minh City cost about ₹1,500–3,000 and cover a sampan ride, coconut-candy workshop and fruit-orchard lunch — fine as a taster, but the delta rewards an overnight. Sleep in Can Tho and reach Cai Rang floating market by 6am, when wholesale boats trade pineapples and pumpkins off their bows; it winds down by 8. Cycle the island lanes of Ben Tre between visits. The delta is hot and humid year-round, so mornings are everything here. Homestays among the orchards from around ₹1,800 a night make it the cheapest immersion in Vietnam.

image.alt: Boats laden with produce at the Cai Rang floating market on the Mekong

highlights.name: Sapa rice terraces & Fansipan
highlights.blurb: Cascading rice terraces carved into misty mountains near the Chinese border, with a cable car to Indochina's highest peak.
highlights.detail: Sapa is a 5.5-hour expressway drive or overnight sleeper bus from Hanoi. Base in town or, better, in a Ta Van valley homestay, and walk village-to-village with a local Hmong or Red Dao guide — day treks run about ₹1,200–2,000 and support the communities directly. The terraces are mirror-flooded in May–June and blaze gold in mid-September, the two most photogenic windows; December–February gets genuinely cold, occasionally with frost. The Fansipan cable car (about ₹2,600) shortcuts a two-day climb into 20 minutes, sunrise-clear most often in October–November. Two nights minimum makes the journey worthwhile.

image.alt: Layered green rice terraces descending into the Muong Hoa valley near Sapa

highlights.name: Phong Nha caves
highlights.blurb: The world's biggest cave systems hide under this national park — from easy boat rides into Phong Nha cave to swims through Hang Toi's dark passages.
highlights.detail: Phong Nha-Ke Bang sits between Hanoi and Hue, reachable by sleeper bus or via Dong Hoi's airport and station. Paradise Cave's first kilometre of boardwalk past colossal formations is the accessible showstopper; the Phong Nha cave boat ride glides straight into the mountain; and Hang Toi adds zip lines, mud baths and headlamp swims for the adventurous. Hardcore cavers can book the two-day Hang En trek — camping inside a cave with its own beach — while Son Doong, the world's largest, books out a year ahead at serious expense. Two nights in the laid-back farmstay scene covers the highlights; roads are prettiest February to August.

image.alt: Vast illuminated stalactite formations inside Paradise Cave, Phong Nha

highlights.name: Hue Imperial City
highlights.blurb: The moated citadel of Vietnam's last emperors, with royal tombs scattered along the Perfume River — the country's most atmospheric history stop.
highlights.detail: Hue is two hours from Da Nang over the Hai Van Pass, itself a highlight worth doing by car or motorbike rather than the tunnel. Give the Imperial City a full morning from 8am — the roughly ₹700 ticket covers the restored Thai Hoa Palace, royal theatre and long brick corridors that survived the war. In the afternoon pick two tombs: Khai Dinh for its wild mosaic interiors and Tu Duc for its lakeside gardens. Combo tickets save money if you visit three sites. Eat like an emperor cheaply — bun bo Hue and banh khoai are local dishes worth planning a lunch around. One night is enough; two is unhurried.

image.alt: The Meridian Gate entrance to Hue's walled Imperial City

activities.name: Overnight cruise in Ha Long or Lan Ha Bay
activities.blurb: Sleep on the water among limestone towers, with kayaking, cave stops, squid fishing off the stern and a sunrise tai chi session on deck.

image.alt: Kayakers paddling between karst islands near a cruise boat in Lan Ha Bay

activities.name: Guided street-food crawl
activities.blurb: Eat where locals queue — pho, bun cha, banh xeo and egg coffee across six or seven stops in Hanoi or Saigon, often from the back of a vintage Vespa.

image.alt: Steaming bowls of pho being served at a busy Hanoi pavement stall

activities.name: Hai Van Pass by motorbike or jeep
activities.blurb: Ride the coastal mountain road Top Gear made famous, between Hue and Hoi An, with easy-rider drivers available if you'd rather sit back and watch the coast unfurl.

image.alt: The Hai Van Pass road curving along mountains above the sea

activities.name: Cooking class with market tour
activities.blurb: Shop the morning market with a chef, boat down the river, then roll your own fresh spring rolls and banh xeo in a Hoi An garden kitchen — most classes handle vegetarians happily.

image.query: hoi an cooking class spring rolls
image.alt: Travellers rolling fresh spring rolls at an outdoor Hoi An cooking class

activities.name: Spa and hot-spring afternoon
activities.blurb: Ninety-minute massages for under ₹1,500, herbal baths of the Red Dao people in Sapa, and mud baths in Nha Trang — recovery days here cost less than a Mumbai facial.

image.alt: A traditional wooden herbal bath tub at a Vietnamese spa

activities.name: Saigon rooftop and craft-beer night
activities.blurb: Start with sunset cocktails above the District 1 skyline, work through the city's surprisingly serious craft breweries, and end amid the chaos of Bui Vien walking street.

image.alt: A rooftop bar overlooking the lit-up Ho Chi Minh City skyline at night

trips.title: Northern Classic
trips.summary: The north's greatest hits in one tight loop: Old Quarter street food and Train Street from a Hanoi base, a night among Ninh Binh's karsts with a dawn Trang An boat ride, then an overnight cruise through Ha Long Bay before flying home from Hanoi.

image.alt: Sunset over karst islands from the deck of a Ha Long Bay cruise

trips.title: Heritage Coast
trips.summary: Central Vietnam at an easy pace: beach time and the Golden Bridge from Da Nang, three lantern-lit nights in Hoi An with a cooking class and tailoring, then over the Hai Van Pass to Hue's Imperial City and royal tombs. Fly into Da Nang non-stop-adjacent via a short hop.

image.alt: Lantern-lit boats on the Thu Bon river in Hoi An at night

trips.title: Grand Vietnam
trips.summary: Top to bottom with cheap domestic flights doing the long legs: Hanoi and a Ha Long cruise, Hoi An's old town and beaches, then the south for Cu Chi Tunnels, rooftop nights in Saigon and a floating-market morning in the Mekong Delta before flying home.

image.alt: A collage-worthy view of Vietnam's landscapes from karst bays to city skylines

faqs.q: Do Indians need a visa for Vietnam?
faqs.a: Yes — an e-visa, applied entirely online at the official evisa.gov.vn portal. It costs USD 25 (about ₹2,200) for single entry, allows stays up to 90 days, and typically takes 3–5 working days to approve. Apply at least 10 days before flying and carry a printout.

faqs.q: Will I find vegetarian food easily?
faqs.a: Yes, with a little vocabulary. 'An chay' means vegetarian, and every town has Buddhist com chay eateries serving full veg meals for ₹100–200. Big cities have Indian restaurants too. Watch for fish sauce in dressings — ask for it left out, and cooking classes will happily run veg versions.

faqs.q: How much does a Vietnam trip cost from India?
faqs.a: With non-stop flights often at ₹15,000–22,000 return, a comfortable 7-night trip lands around ₹55,000–70,000 per person including hotels, food and activities. Backpackers manage on ₹40,000; on the ground Vietnam is meaningfully cheaper than Thailand or Bali.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: November to April suits most itineraries — cool and dry in the north, sunny in the south. Central beaches peak February to August. Avoid planning around Tet (late January–mid February most years) unless you want the festival itself, as transport and shops shut for days.

faqs.q: How do I get around between cities?
faqs.a: Domestic flights on VietJet or Vietnam Airlines cover Hanoi–Da Nang–Ho Chi Minh City from about ₹2,500–4,000 when booked early. Sleeper trains and open-tour buses handle shorter hops cheaply, and Grab replaces haggling with taxis inside cities. Long-distance self-drive is not practical for visitors.
